sources.rank_basis: The TypeScript project's own documentation site (typescriptlang.org/docs/).
MDN Web Docs under developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/, a curated secondary reference, not the ECMAScript spec.
The V8 blog (v8.dev/blog/) is named as Rank 4 engineering literature; it could also be read as the implementer's own publication (Rank 1), so the higher number is taken.
Node.js official API documentation (nodejs.org/api/), served as the v26.13.1 docs with a version history table.

claim_checks.claim: `private` and `protected` are enforced only during type checking. Runtime lookups, and bracket notation even during type checking, still reach the member: it is "soft private".
claim_checks.page_says: private and protected are only enforced during type checking. … private also allows access using bracket notation during type checking … these fields are soft private
claim_checks.note: Runtime lookup is stated for both private and protected; the bracket-notation escape and the 'soft private' label are stated for private only. Read as describing a private member, which the label implies, the claim holds. Wording 'a `private` member' would remove the ambiguity.

claim_checks.claim: `#` fields stay private after compilation and have no bracket-notation escape hatch: they are "hard private".
claim_checks.page_says: JavaScript’s private fields (#) remain private after compilation and do not provide the previously mentioned escape hatches like bracket notation access, making them hard private.

claim_checks.claim: When compiling to ES2021 or lower, TypeScript replaces `#` with `WeakMap`s. The handbook notes that these runtime privacy checks could affect performance.
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #. … Note that these added privacy checks during runtime could affect performance.
claim_checks.note: The modal 'could' is kept. The handbook's caveat covers closures, WeakMaps and private fields alike; the doc attaches it to the WeakMap downlevel only, which is a narrowing, not an overstatement.

claim_checks.claim: Private elements are not properties. They cannot be enumerated, deleted, proxied, or reached through `Object` methods, and `structuredClone()` does not copy them.
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method. … structuredClone() does not clone private elements
claim_checks.note: 'Not properties' matches MDN's note that it avoids the term 'private property' because private elements have no key or property attributes.

claim_checks.claim: Reading a `#` field from an object whose class did not declare it throws a `TypeError`. `#x in obj` checks for it without throwing.
claim_checks.page_says: from an object that doesn't have the element, a TypeError is thrown … This will return true if the private field or method exists, and false otherwise.
claim_checks.note: The example's error text is 'Cannot read private member #x from an object whose class did not declare it'.

claim_checks.claim: V8 9.7 moved class-field initialization, including private fields, onto its inline-cache fast path. Before that it went through slower runtime calls.
claim_checks.page_says: With v9.7, when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough, it uses a new IC to speed up the operation … falls back to a runtime call
claim_checks.note: The second sentence holds ('Before v9.7, V8 always used a costly runtime call'). The first drops the page's condition: the IC fast path is taken only when the initialization pattern is predictable, and V8 falls back to a runtime call for unseen patterns, proxy targets, existing fields or unseen hidden classes. Unqualified, it reads as all class-field initialization now being fast, which also props up the Summary's equal-cost statement.

claim_checks.claim: Object wrapped in a `Proxy` … `#` access does not go through the proxy | Private elements cannot be proxied
claim_checks.page_says: they cannot be proxied, enumerated, deleted, or interacted with using any Object method.
claim_checks.note: The page does not describe what a call through a proxy then does (in practice a TypeError when the proxy is the receiver); the row's wording stays within what the page says.

claim_checks.claim: Target ES2021 or lower | `#` becomes `WeakMap` lookups | TypeScript downlevels it
claim_checks.page_says: When compiling to ES2021 or less, TypeScript will use WeakMaps in place of #.

claim_checks.claim: Working around it with `--experimental-transform-types` | Runs on Node 24.22 with an `ExperimentalWarning` (re-tested 2026-11-03); the flag is removed in Node 26.0.0 | So code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as `readonly #field`s assigned in the constructor
claim_checks.note: The removal is in the v26.0.0 history row (entails), and the page lists parameter properties among features that need transformation. The ExperimentalWarning on Node 24.22 is a local re-test the page does not cover. The cell the ✅ closes is the doc's own recommendation to use `readonly #` fields; the page says nothing about private fields (a declared `private readonly x` assigned in the constructor would be erasable too). Searched: 'private', '#', 'readonly', 'ExperimentalWarning'.

claim_checks.claim: Type stripping itself | Stable (stability 2) since Node 24.12.0 and 25.2.0; no warning since 24.3.0; Node ignores `tsconfig.json` and needs `.ts` extensions in relative imports | Node only deletes types
claim_checks.page_says: Type stripping is now stable. … Type stripping no longer emits an experimental warning. … Since Node.js is only removing inline types
claim_checks.note: Stability 2 since v25.2.0/v24.12.0, tsconfig.json ignored, mandatory file extensions and 'only removing inline types' all entail. 'No warning since 24.3.0' drops the qualifier: the page says no experimental warning (since v24.3.0 and v22.18.0), not no warning of any kind. Judged on the whole row because the References entry says [^4] backs these version facts.

conflicts.topic: Runtime cost of # fields: the Summary states as fact that # fields cost the same as public fields on any native ES2022+ target, from one local run (Node 24.22, V8 13.6); [^1] says runtime privacy checks, private fields included, 'could affect performance', and [^3] says the IC fast path applies only to predictable patterns. The rank 1 text is a hedge, not a contrary value, so this is a scoping gap (see the Summary SOFT_WARN), not an unarbitrated conflict.

violations.evidence: C6 overstates [^3]: item 6 drops the condition 'when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough' and the runtime-call fallback.
C9 unsupported by [^4]: the ✅ closes the doc's own recommendation (keep collaborators as readonly # fields), which the Node page does not state; the Node 24.22 ExperimentalWarning is a local re-test.
C10 overstates [^4]: 'no warning since 24.3.0' for a page that says 'no longer emits an experimental warning'.

The Summary ('On a native ES2022+ target, reading and creating # fields costs the same as public fields') and Takeaways ('measured cost is nil') state an unmarked fact generalized from one local run on Node 24.22 / V8 13.6 to every native ES2022+ target, with neither ✅ nor ⚠️, while [^3] limits the fast path to predictable patterns and [^1] cautions that runtime privacy checks could affect performance.

The 'Where each form fits' table is decision guidance, not mechanism, inside the role 3 section, and it carries an unmarked, uncited fact ('A # name cannot be a parameter (TypeScript error TS18009)') that the Verification status count does not include.

patch_instructions.action: Replace item 6 with: 'V8 9.7 extended its inline-cache (IC) system to class-field initialization, private fields included. When the initialization pattern is predictable enough, V8 takes the IC fast path; otherwise (for example an unseen hidden class, a proxy target or a field that already exists) it falls back to a runtime call. Before 9.7 it always used a costly runtime call. ✅[^3]' — supported by [^3]: 'when V8 considers the pattern of the initialization to be predictable enough, it uses a new IC' and 'it falls back to a runtime call to deal with the slow cases'.

In the `--experimental-transform-types` row, put ✅[^4] right after 'the flag is **removed in Node 26.0.0**' (v26.0.0 history row of [^4]); label 'Runs on Node 24.22 with an ExperimentalWarning (re-tested 2026-11-03)' as a local re-test with no ✅; and remove the ✅[^4] from the Why cell, which is the doc's own recommendation, or rewrite it as 'Type stripping rejects parameter properties ✅[^4], so code meant to run unbuilt keeps injected collaborators as fields assigned in the constructor (this doc uses `readonly #`)'.

In the 'Type stripping itself' row, change 'no warning since 24.3.0' to 'no experimental warning since 24.3.0 (and 22.18.0)', per the [^4] history row 'Type stripping no longer emits an experimental warning.'

Scope the performance sentence to what was measured, for example 'Measured on Node 24.22 (V8 13.6) with a native ES2023 target, reading and creating # fields cost the same as public fields', and mark it as a local measurement; make the matching change to the second Takeaway. Add an Edge cases row that V8 takes the IC fast path only for predictable initialization patterns ✅[^3] and that the TypeScript handbook cautions that runtime privacy checks could affect performance ✅[^1].
Move the 'Where each form fits' table to ## Trade-offs (it is a decision table), and either cite a source for 'TypeScript error TS18009' with ✅ or mark it ⚠️ and count it in ## Verification status.
